introduction: A visitor asked ‘Abdu’l-Bahá whether it was good to wear a cross. “It concentrates your thoughts,” he said; “it has no magical power.” The readings apply the same sense to fortune-telling, the evil eye, seances, automatic writing and talismans: most of what is claimed comes from the mind of the person concerned, real communion is of the heart, and attention is better spent on keeping one’s own glass clean. The Hebrew prophets were as dry about diviners and stargazers; Epictetus, Hobbes and Shakespeare’s Edmund make the psychological point; the fringes of Numbers and the doorposts of Deuteronomy are reminders of the kind the readings approve. Other passages complicate the picture. Saul did go to Endor, Paul will not explain his own rapture, Ephesians treats dark powers as real, and Hezekiah had to destroy a sacred object once people began to burn incense to it.
questions: A ring or a cross is “a reminder, and companion,” with no magic in it. Hezekiah broke the brazen serpent when it was worshipped. How would you know if a reminder of yours had become something else?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the evil eye works on the one who believes in it, and Epictetus that we are disturbed by our views of things. What fears in your own surroundings work this way?
The readings call spirit messages delusion and yet affirm that “spirit can communicate with spirit,” as in teaching. What is the difference they are drawing?
“By what means can one determine that what has entered his heart is divine inspiration?” Compare the reading’s answer with John’s “try the spirits” and Hobbes’s scepticism.

A talisman is said to be effective when used with purity of heart and sincere intention; the Ephesians burned their books of charms. Where would you draw the line between prayerful use of a sign and superstition?

outside.why: Fortune-telling is “the domain of … diviners, not of the righteous.” Deuteronomy’s list is longer and its ban flat: there shall not be found among you any one that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter.

A cross or a ring “has no magical power”; it is “a reminder, and companion.” The fringe on the garments of Israel is commanded for that reason and no other: that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments.

Asked about clairvoyance, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of living in the body as in a clean glass case. Jesus: the light of the body is the eye; if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
The evil eye harms the one “who believes and is convinced.” Epictetus’s general rule: men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.

Divination and geomancy are forbidden, so that no deceiver may wear “the cloth of trustworthiness.” Isaiah to Babylon: let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee.

Bahá’u’lláh challenges a claimant to bring his science “from the realm of fancy to the domain of fact.” Ben Jonson’s comedy of 1610 shows the customer of such a science on the morning he expects his gold: this day, thou shalt have ingots.
“If it were true … every government would choose someone to communicate with spirits.” Isaiah’s objection to mediums is as dry: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?

The reading supposes that no government consults spirits. King Saul, who had banned the practice, went in disguise to the woman at Endor on the night before his last battle. What does a ruler’s resort to it show about the practice, or about him?

Automatic writing comes from “the human spirit … within the self of the one doing the writing.” Hobbes on reported messages: to say he hath spoken to him in a dream is no more than to say he dreamed that God spake to him.
Control by unseen forces “is but the imagination of mankind.” Edmund in King Lear: this is the excellent foppery of the world, that we make guilty of our disasters the sun, the moon, and the stars.

Evil forces are dismissed as imagination. Ephesians takes them in earnest: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against the rulers of the darkness of this world. Are the two speaking of the same thing under different names?

“By what means can one determine that what has entered his heart is divine inspiration?” The First Letter of John asks for a test and gives one: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.

Rappings and table-turning are “material things”; what counts is “the character and the heart.” Abraham in Jesus’s parable: if they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.

Stories of the spirit projected out of the body are called “fantastic hyperboles.” Paul reports such a thing soberly and refuses to explain it: whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth. How should a claim of this kind be held?

A talisman or the Name dissolved in water is effective if done “with complete attention, purity of heart, sincere intention.” The woman who touched Jesus’s garment was told where the power lay: daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole.

The reading allows the wearing of talismans under conditions. At Ephesus many which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men. Where is the line between a devout sign and a charm?
“Place the Greatest Name in your dwelling, wear the ring.” Israel is told of the words of the law: bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and write them upon the posts of thy house.

A name on the wall and a ring on the hand, to make superstitious influences “vanish away.” Hezekiah broke in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made, because the people had come to burn incense to it. What keeps a reminder from becoming an idol?

isaiah-for-the-living-to-the-dead.text: And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead

deuteronomy-posts-of-thy-house.text: And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates

mark-thy-faith-hath-made-thee-whole.text: When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole … And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague
